summary: For Jamal, Duolingo is an invaluable tool to expand his English vocabulary, but it sometimes lacks the depth needed for contextual understanding.
top_quotes: Duolingo is like, really helpful for learning new words, but sometimes I wish it explains more about context.
It's like having a little teacher in my pocket, you know? But sometimes the lessons feel a bit repetitive.
I like that I can do it anytime, but, uh, I wish it had more speaking exercises.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey, uh, nice to meet you! I'm Jamal.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Ah, where to start, um, I was born in Morocco, and I grew up speaking both Arabic and French, which is kinda common there. Moved to France a few years ago, and living here has been such a, like, big change for me. I love learning languages, so I started with English to make life easier here and for travel, you know? I work part-time while finishing my studies, just trying to balance everything.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in a small town in Morocco, it’s called Chefchaouen. It's really beautiful, known for its, like, blue walls. It’s quite a peaceful place.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was nice actually. Very community-oriented, everyone knows everyone. We didn’t have much, but we had each other, you know? There’s a simplicity to life there that I miss sometimes. It was always about family and friends.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Um, definitely when I moved to France. That was huge for me. It was like stepping into a whole new world. I had to learn to be independent, you know, and adapt quickly to a different culture and language.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because, I mean, everything changed. Suddenly, I had to be responsible for myself in a way I hadn’t been before. It pushed me to learn new skills, like better French at first and then English, because it’s so international here.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Well, um, I took it one step at a time. I focused on integrating myself into the local community, making friends, you know? I also, like, enrolled in language classes and used apps like Duolingo to improve my English.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'd say building a stable future is, like, top priority. I'm really focused on my studies and learning English to open up more opportunities, both here in France and maybe abroad, you know?

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Well, having a good grasp of English, it’s like a key, you know? It opens doors to better jobs and it’s super useful when traveling or working with international companies.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day, um, would be when I manage to wake up early, have a productive study session, maybe practice some English, and then spend some time with friends. If I can also fit in some football, that’s perfect!

interview_script.question: What makes you say 'this was a good day'?
interview_script.answer: When I feel like I did something meaningful, you know? Like, if I learned something new or made progress towards my goals, and had some good laughs with friends.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Um, usually I think things through a lot. I talk to my family or friends for advice - they always give, like, good perspectives. Then I consider what feels right for me in the long term.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, I'm kinda in-between. I like to plan some things ahead, like my studies, but also leave space for spontaneous moments, you know?

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Sure, like, I’ll plan my study schedule for the week, but if a friend calls me up for a last-minute coffee or football match, I’ll totally go for it. Balance is key, I think.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to evaluate the situation first. If I feel like the benefits outweigh the risks and I have a solid backup plan, I go for it. Moving to France was a big risk, but it was worth it, you know?

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Well, I usually wake up around 7 or 8, have some breakfast, and head to class or work, depending on the day. In the afternoon, I try to squeeze in some English practice with Duolingo, maybe meet up with friends, and then in the evening, catch up on my studies or watch a bit of TV to relax.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Uh, definitely the classes and studying part. It can be exhausting trying to switch between languages all the time, you know? But it’s necessary for my goals.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, I wish I had more time to travel and explore France more. There are so many beautiful places I haven’t seen yet. And, uh, more energy for, like, improving my English further.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Last year, I’d say, it was COVID restrictions. It made things really difficult with classes going online and limited social interactions. It was hard to stay motivated sometimes, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I tried to adapt by setting a routine and staying connected with my friends online. We had, like, video calls, and I used Duolingo more to keep practicing English since I had more time at home.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: Um, definitely my family back in Morocco and a few close friends here in France. We’ve been through a lot together, and they know me really well.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: My family, they are like my rock, always supportive and understanding. With my friends, it’s more about shared experiences and, you know, just having fun and supporting each other.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Mostly at university or at my part-time job. But I try to spend weekends with friends or, like, exploring the city.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Uh, at university, I feel focused but sometimes, like, a bit stressed. At work, it’s more relaxed because I’m getting hands-on experience. With friends, I just feel happy and free, you know?

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: The environment, I guess. Like, being at university, the pressure to perform is there. But when I’m with friends, it’s all about enjoying the moment and having fun.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually talk to my elder brother. He always gives practical advice and has been through similar experiences, so, like, he helps me see things clearly.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: There was this time when I felt really overwhelmed with studies and work. There were deadlines piling up, and I was tired from juggling so many things.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: I was really stressed and, like, couldn’t focus well. It was hard to keep up with everything, and I felt a bit down because I wasn’t performing at my best.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I decided to, like, take a step back, reset my schedule, and prioritize things. I also talked to my friends and family for support - they really helped me get through it.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a break and doing something I enjoy, like playing football or listening to music. It clears my mind and gives me a fresh perspective, you know?

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: In a few years, I hope to have a stable career, probably in something international where I can use my languages. I’d like to travel more and maybe, like, live in different countries. That’s the dream.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be more confident with my English, maybe even learn another language. Also, to have more time for myself and my interests outside of work and studies.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: I mostly relied on, like, textbooks and classroom courses. They were okay but sometimes too rigid. I also tried watching English movies and listening to music, which was fun but not very structured, you know?

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Uh, it was the lack of flexibility. I mean, you had to follow the textbook and go at the teacher’s pace. Plus, I didn’t get enough practice for speaking, which is really important for me.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: There was this exam, and I realized I didn’t remember much of what I’d learned because it didn’t, like, stick. I didn’t have enough practice or real-world context to understand fully.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: A friend of mine mentioned it. He was using it to learn Spanish, and he thought it was pretty cool, so I decided to give it a try, you know?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I was curious about its approach. I liked the idea of learning vocabulary through short lessons and gamification. Plus, I could do it anytime, which was perfect for my schedule.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Sure, so, uh, last night, I opened Duolingo before bed. I decided to do a quick vocabulary lesson. It started with a few new words in English and some matching exercises. Then, there was a short story segment where I had to fill in the blanks. It was like, fun and interactive. I liked the immediate feedback - it tells you right away if you’re correct or need to try again. I finished a couple of lessons, then checked my progress with the streak feature, which, like, motivates me to keep going.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: Um, definitely the vocabulary exercises. They really help expand my word knowledge quickly. I enjoy the variety - matching, fill-in-the-blank, even listening exercises are, like, great for reinforcing what I've learned.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes it feels repetitive, you know? Like, I get it, practice is important, but occasionally I wish there was more variety or maybe deeper explanations of grammar. And, uh, less repetitive sentences.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, the repetition can be annoying after a while. I wish it switched up the exercises more often and, um, included more complex sentences. Sometimes I feel like I'm not being challenged enough, especially with context.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was this one time, I kept seeing the same few words and sentences, and it got boring, you know? I felt like I wasn’t progressing anymore. It was frustrating, and I considered switching to another app for a bit to get a different approach.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Kind of. Sometimes I complement Duolingo with watching English movies or listening to podcasts. It helps me with, like, context and natural usage of language that Duolingo doesn’t always provide.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They, like, provide context and real-life usage. You know, how people actually speak and use expressions - that's really important to me. Plus, it helps with pronunciation and, uh, listening skills.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Hmm, worst-case? I guess not being able to improve or use English effectively when I need it most, like in a job interview or while traveling. That would be pretty frustrating after all the time spent learning.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it, like, gives me new words or phrases to learn. I want it to challenge me a bit and help me feel like I’m progressing in my English journey, you know?

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I'm, like, able to recall new words easily and use them in conversations, that’s a good sign. Also, if I can understand more in podcasts or movies, it means Duolingo helped a lot.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d add more speaking exercises, you know? Practice with pronunciation is really important, and it could help users build confidence in speaking English.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I’d love to see a more personalized approach in language learning apps, like tailored lessons that adapt to the user’s level and needs to make it more effective.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Not that I can think of, but, uh, I think we covered a lot about my experience. It’s been interesting to think about how I learn languages.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Uh, sure, as long as it respects my privacy and is used for good purposes, I’m okay with it.
